cim: More Madison area businesses are adopting AI, survey finds
cim_eredeti: More Madison area businesses are adopting AI, survey finds
szoveg_eredeti:
About 83% of surveyed businesses used artificial intelligence this year, up from 51% two years ago, the 2026 Next Normal Regional employer survey found.

The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning.

An annual survey of businesses in the Madison area found a continued rise in the use of artificial intelligence this year.

The 2026 Next Normal Regional Employer survey collected responses from 218 businesses across the state from Sept. 2 to Sept. 22.

About 83% reported using AI, up from 79% last year and 51% two years ago. The uptick in AI usage this year was “expected” and mirrored results from previous surveys, said Kevin Little, vice president of the Greater Madison Chamber of Commerce, who helped oversee the data collection.

The increase also came as no surprise to Moses Altsech, a teaching professor of marketing at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s business school. Altsech said he’s long observed an increasing share of businesses “jumping on the bandwagon” in fear of being “left behind.”

However, he added, it’s been difficult to fully quantify and understand the impact of this upward trend in AI usage for these businesses.

“Adoption of AI and successful implementation of AI (are) not the same thing, so I wonder what AI has done for these businesses in terms of results. Has it improved productivity? Are you saving time? Are you increasing profits? Are your customers happier because you spend more time with them?” Altsech said.

Altsech isn’t yet convinced businesses have been able to meaningfully leverage AI. One issue he’s seen raised in research is that while AI might increase efficiency in one area, employers will often give employees more responsibilities to fill that extra time, meaning they actually work longer hours than before AI was introduced.

He said AI chatbots can significantly slow down customer service interactions, too.

“We're not really thinking about how this ad hoc use of AI is affecting our people, their workday, and our customers' experience, and I think either businesses are going to start thinking about that, or they're going to pay a price for it sooner or later,” Altsech said.

Zach Brandon, president of the Greater Madison Chamber of Commerce, offered an alternative perspective, saying the Chamber’s use of an AI to take over scheduling allowed the organization to promote the individual who had been handling scheduling. That employee now has received additional training, works on more complex operations-related tasks and advanced their career.

As companies navigate the budding AI landscape, Brandon emphasized the importance of companies quelling employees' fears around human workforces being replaced by technology.

“We should all be thinking about how (AI is) an accelerant to human potential, not a replacement for human capability,” Brandon said.

So far, Little said, AI remains at a “pretty minimal” level of workplace integration both locally and nationally.

This year’s survey listed administrative support as the top use for AI among businesses that reported using AI this year. About 72% reported using AI for that purpose, down four percentage points from last year, and 54% of businesses still reported AI is “minimally integrated” into workflows.

While the study does not define “administrative support,” Brandon clarified the term likely alludes to businesses using AI for simpler tasks related to scheduling and emailing.

AI assistance in writing and sending emails has been the “bleeding edge” of administrative support, Brandon said. He’s noticed people feel especially comfortable using AI for that purpose because it feels like a familiar and natural progression from spell-check softwares that are already commonly used with emails.

Adding AI to an email service doesn’t take much integration so it’s a lower effort and less intrusive addition for employees to take on, Brandon said.

Among respondents who said they did not use AI, the most cited reasons at 48% each were privacy and security concerns as well as AI not being applicable to their business.

Along with AI use, the survey asked respondents about barriers to their business this year. Economic uncertainty came out on top at 61%, and healthcare costs jumped to 42%, up 14 percentage points from last year, to become the third-leading barrier.

Altsech said he hopes research on the economic impact of AI continues to expand in order to demystify how AI is, in practice, changing employee productivity and satisfaction as well as consumer behavior. More qualitative studies would be particularly “interesting to really parse out,” Altsech said.

“(AI is) not going away, and it's not a fad, and it's not a trend, and it has value, but we're still not at the stage where we're capitalizing on it,” Altsech said.
